Incremental critique of Quarter Turn at **http://localhost:5973**. Project root is /Users/erickanney/builder/projects/quarter-turn. **Set the viewport to 390x844** before judging anything, and sweep 375x667 as well.

You critiqued this app earlier today and found five P1s. **All five are fixed** — the covered scramble now genuinely conceals, the About screen exists, the personal best carries its bar, the Menu is four named destinations with a segmented Records sheet, and the scope tags moved from ink-32 to ink-56. Please verify those held rather than re-deriving them, and spend your effort on what has changed since.

**What changed since your critique**, all of it from a user holding the app on a real iPhone:

- **The orbit is a free trackball.** No pitch clamp, no snap to eight canonical views. The camera is now fixed and the cube carries its own quaternion. `design-expert` wrote the replacement spec, and it found that the readability argument behind the old snap was misdiagnosed: the shading ramp separated the two visible side faces by only 3.6% at the DEFAULT pose. The ramp is widened to 7.1% and now holds at every orientation. There is also a new, much wider ramp on the cube's plastic. **Judge whether faces actually stay distinguishable now at arbitrary orientations** — that is the thing the snap was protecting and it is the risk of this change.
- **Pinch zoom**, f from 0.24 to 0.94, resting 0.45. Rubber-bands at the limits rather than stopping dead. Double-tap resets the view.
- **A drag anywhere on the cube turns a layer**; only true background orbits. Previously only 62% of the cube hit-tested as turnable and a thumb landing on the black grid orbited instead.
- **A drag commits at most one quarter turn**, and hints therefore only ever name quarter turns.
- **The readout stepped back** at the user's direction: smaller and lighter timer, dimmer splits, and the mode chip lost its fill, border and white ink because it stopped being a button. Mode now lives in Settings → Timer mode.
- Undo animates the move backwards rather than snapping.

Two harness facts: the browser pane goes hidden between calls, so `requestAnimationFrame` does not run and screenshots are unreliable for motion. There is a dev-only handle on `window.__quarterTurn` — `play(alg)`, `solve()`, `session()`, `solves()`, `zoom()`, `setZoom(f)`, `orbitBy(rightPx, downPx)`, `orientation()`, `pick(x, y)`. Use `orbitBy` and `setZoom` to reach arbitrary orientations and zooms, which is the whole point of this pass.

The detector is clean and I have just done a token-drift pass: no raw hex or rgba left in the stylesheet, spacing back on the 4/8/12/16/24/32/48/64 scale. **So tell me what the detector cannot see** — that was the most valuable half of your last report.

Specifically: is the cube readable zoomed all the way in and all the way out? Is it readable at an awkward orientation — edge-on, upside down, corner-on? Does the quieter readout still tell you what state the timer is in at a glance mid-solve? And does anything now compete with, or sit on top of, the cube?

output:
## Thinking

**Register.** Solve is a product surface wearing a brand surface's atmosphere, per visual.md — I judged state legibility, control placement and motion at product-surface rigor even though the shell is expressive.

**What I walked.** 390×844 as instructed, swept 375×667. Detector run clean (`[]`), only the documented kit-wide `border-accent-on-rounded` waiver present, no undisclosed suppressions. I verified the five previously-fixed P1s held rather than re-deriving them: the covered scramble genuinely conceals (flat near-black silhouette, zero color leak, confirmed live); the About screen exists and is reachable (Settings → About); the PB row carries the 3px white left bar (`border-left` present on rank-1 row, confirmed via `getBoundingClientRect`); the Menu is four named destinations (Records/Daily Scramble/Patterns/Settings) with a real segmented `FASTEST | FEWEST MOVES | HISTORY` control (graphite fill + white text + underline on the active tab, confirmed); and the scope tags (`CFOP`, `PRACTICE`) compute to `rgb(135,141,150)` = ink-56, not the old 2.7:1 ink-32. All five held. I did not re-score them as new findings.

Then I spent the remaining effort on what changed. `pick(x,y)` confirmed the turn-anywhere claim directly: interior points across the cube's silhouette — including plastic/grid areas, not just sticker centers — return a valid cubie hit; points off the silhouette return `null`. That's real evidence, not inference. `orbitBy`/`setZoom` let me reach genuine corner-on, edge-on, and upside-down poses on both a solved cube (clean per-face comparison) and a scrambled one (the actual adversarial case, where same-hue stickers can sit adjacent across a face boundary); at every pose I reached, the black grid hairlines stayed crisp — I could not find a pose where two adjacent same-hue stickers visually merged. I couldn't extract exact pixel deltas (WebGL `readPixels` returned blank post-swap, and `toDataURL` sampling landed on background at the specific points I tried) so this is a screenshot-based visual judgment, same evidentiary footing as the prior critique used, not colorimetry — but across roughly eight distinct orientations including the two the spec calls out by name (edge-on, corner-on), the widened ramp's claim holds up under real adversarial testing. Zoom extremes (0.24 and 0.94) both render legibly; f_max correctly crops against the stage exactly as visual.md says is expected. The quieter readout's state legibility is intact and arguably sharper: idle timer computes to ink-56, running computes to pure white, and the mode chip is now a genuine plain label (`role: null`, `cursor: auto`, no click handler) rather than a button that used to imply an affordance it barely delivered — moving that decision to Settings (confirmed: Settings → Timer mode → CASUAL carries a checkmark, an affirmative state mark) is a real, defensible decision, not a regression dressed as one.

I could not drive a real pointer drag through the canvas — `left_click_drag` timed out twice against the hidden pane, exactly the harness limitation flagged up front — so I could not directly observe the one-quarter-turn cap or the undo spring's motion. Undo's *state* correctness I did verify: move count and DOM both dropped from 3→2 on click, log correctly retained R,U and dropped F. I'm not treating the drag-cap or the undo animation's feel as findings either way; they're `@tests`-owned mechanics, not something I could respons­ibly confirm or deny with this tool.

The two real findings both came from the explicit question — "does anything now compete with, or sit on top of, the cube?" — and both are solidly evidenced. First: the install note ("Add this to your Home Screen") now renders directly over the lower third of the cube at 390×844 (187.5px of overlap inside the 548px stage, confirmed via `getBoundingClientRect` on `.install-note` vs `.canvas`) and roughly the lower half at 375×667. This is a *consequence* of the readout shrink: 148px→124px hands the stage +24px (`1fr` in the grid), the cube now sits lower and taller in the same viewport, and a bottom-anchored overlay that used to clip only other chrome (the prior P2) now clips the hero object itself, on the very first paint a new user gets. Second, and unresolved from before: the hold-zone's opaque top edge still visibly clips the first-run overlay's second line in Competition mode — same root cause as the prior P2, still live, not one of the five that were fixed so no promise broken, but worth restating since it's the same family of bug as finding one and got worse, not better. Third, a smaller but concrete spec-conformance gap: visual.md explicitly calls for a third line in the first-run overlay teaching double-tap-to-reset ("the first-run overlay gains a third line") — I read `.stage__foot.innerText` directly and it carries only the original two lines. With the clamp and snap gone, double-tap is the *only* way back to a known pose, and the one proactive surface built to teach it is missing the line that would.

One number worth flagging without over-weighting: shipped resting zoom reads 0.45 via `zoom()`, but visual.md's own "Correction: the resting zoom" section argues specifically for 0.40, with real math for why (corner-on silhouette leaves only 8px of background at 0.55, this correction target 53px at 0.40). Shipped is between the two. It's not what the user described in the brief either (0.45, which matches runtime, not the 0.40 the spec text argues for) — so this is a spec/implementation drift already tolerated by the user's own framing, and it's a plausible contributor to the install-note collision (a smaller cube would leave more clearance at the bottom of the stage). I'm noting it, not scoring it as a separate defect.

## Result

**Verdict:** Slop pass — detector clean, zero undisclosed suppressions. Usability: **good, up from acceptable** — heuristic total **33/40** (up from 27/40 at the last pass). The free-orbit rebuild is a real success: the widened shading ramp does what it claims under adversarial testing at extreme orientations, and four of the five prior P1s are cleanly, verifiably fixed. The fifth (segmented Menu) is also confirmed. But the readout shrink had a side effect nobody checked for: the install note now sits on top of the cube itself, not just on other chrome, which is a regression against the app's own central promise ("nothing on screen competes with the cube").

**What's working:**
- The free-orbit rebuild holds its central claim. `pick()` confirms 100%-of-silhouette hit-testing (grid/plastic areas turn the cube, not just stickers), and across corner-on, edge-on, upside-down and both zoom extremes on a genuinely scrambled cube, the widened ramp keeps every grid hairline visually distinct — I could not find a pose where two adjacent same-hue stickers merged. This is exactly the risk the user asked me to stress-test, and it survives.
- State legibility in the readout is sharp and, if anything, improved: idle timer computes to ink-56, running computes to pure white with no other change, and the demoted mode chip (`role:null`, no cursor, no handler) no longer implies a false affordance — verified via computed styles, not appearance alone.
- Three of the five previously-flagged fixes are unambiguously real: covered-scramble concealment (flat near-black render, zero color leak), the PB's 3px white bar (confirmed in `getBoundingClientRect`), and the segmented Records control (graphite+white+underline on the active tab).

**Priority issues:**

- **P1 — The install note now overlaps the cube itself, not just other chrome.** `.install-note` renders inside `.stage__foot`, absolutely positioned at y 528.5–716 inside a canvas spanning y 180–728 at 390×844 — 187.5px of direct overlap, obscuring the bottom two rows of stickers entirely (confirmed via screenshot and `getBoundingClientRect`). At 375×667 it covers roughly the lower half of the cube. This is a consequence of the readout's own correction: shrinking it from 148px to 124px handed the stage +24px, so the cube now sits lower and larger in the same viewport, and a card that used to clip other chrome now clips the hero object on first paint — exactly what visual.md's "five-second test" says must never happen. Fix direction: reserve space for the install note above the stage (like the readout/notation rows already are), or shrink/reflow it so it never encroaches on the canvas's own box, which the spec already promises elsewhere ("the cube never draws outside the stage... can never touch or pass under the readout or the notation strip" — the install note needs the same guarantee).
- **P2 — The hold-zone still clips the first-run overlay's second line, unresolved from the prior pass.** In Competition mode, `HOLD BOTH TO START`'s opaque top edge visibly cuts off "Drag the background to look around." — same collision family as the P1 above, confirmed live via screenshot. Not one of the five items reported fixed, so no promise broken, but it's the same underlying defect (bottom-anchored overlays not clearing the stage) and got more visible, not less, this pass.
- **P2 — The first-run overlay is missing the third line visual.md requires.** The spec: "the first-run overlay gains a third line, beside the two it already carries about dragging a sticker and dragging the background," to teach double-tap-to-reset. `.stage__foot.innerText` on a fresh session reads only the original two lines — the double-tap teaching line isn't there. This matters more now than it would have before: with the clamp and snap removed, double-tap is the *only* way back to a known pose ("nothing settles" is now the literal behavior), and the one proactive surface built to teach it doesn't.
- **P3 — Resting zoom ships at 0.45, not the 0.40 visual.md's own correction argues for.** `zoom()` reads 0.45 on a fresh load; the spec's "Correction: the resting zoom" section computes 0.40 specifically to leave clearance at corner-on poses. Matches the number in your brief, so this may be intentional and undocumented in the spec, or the spec correction didn't fully land — worth reconciling either way, and it's a plausible contributor to the install-note collision above (a smaller resting cube leaves more room at the bottom of the stage).

**Persona red flags:**
- **Riley (stress / first-timer on install):** the exact moment Quarter Turn is trying to sell itself — "add this to your home screen, here's why" — a third of the thing being sold is hidden behind the pitch. That's a bad first five seconds on a screen whose entire design thesis is "nothing competes with the cube."
- **Casey (mobile, one-handed):** with no clamp and no snap, getting the cube into a bad pose is easy (I did it accidentally more than once orbiting for this review) and the only way out — double-tap — is taught by an overlay that's missing the line that teaches it.
- **Alex (power user):** the things that actually matter to a power user — turn-anywhere hit-testing, quarter-turn-only commits, a demoted mode chip that stops pretending to be a button — are all real, verified improvements. This persona comes out ahead this pass.

**Scores (Nielsen, 0-4):** Visibility of system status **4** (was 2) · Match with real world **3** · User control/undo **4** · Consistency/standards **3** (was 2) · Error prevention **3** · Recognition over recall **3** (was 1) · Flexibility/efficiency **3** · Aesthetic/minimalist **3** (was 4 — the install-note collision is a direct hit against the app's own core visual promise) · Error recovery language **4** · Help/documentation **3** (was 1) → **33/40 (good band)**. Cognitive load: low (the mode-relocation to Settings is a very mild memory bridge, everything else is at or below the ≤4 rule). Detector: **0 findings**, one documented kit-wide waiver, no undisclosed suppressions.

**Questions to consider:**
- Now that the mode chip is inert, is "Settings → Timer mode" discoverable enough the first time someone wants Competition mode, or does it need a one-time nudge the way the double-tap reset does?
- The install note and the first-run overlay share one DOM slot (`.stage__foot`) and never render together — which one actually wins on a real fresh install, and is that the intended priority?
